what_its_for: Halobetasol is a strong steroid cream, ointment, lotion, or foam that helps relieve redness, itching, swelling, and irritation caused by certain skin conditions such as psoriasis and eczema (dermatitis). It works by calming down the immune response in your skin.
how_to_take: Wash your hands before and after applying this medicine. Apply a thin layer to the affected skin area and gently rub it in. Do not bandage, wrap, or cover the treated area tightly unless your doctor tells you to. Keep this medicine away from your eyes, nose, mouth, and groin area. Do not use it on broken, infected, or open skin unless directed by your doctor. Use only on the skin — do not swallow it.
dosing: Use halobetasol exactly as your doctor prescribes. It is usually applied once or twice daily. Do not use it more often or for longer than directed. Because it is a very strong steroid, most doctors limit use to 2 weeks or less. Do not apply it to large areas of your body without your doctor's approval.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, apply it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not apply extra medicine to make up for a missed dose.
storage: Store halobetasol at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Keep it out of reach of children and pets. Do not freeze the lotion or foam. If you have leftover or expired medicine, ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid getting halobetasol in your eyes, mouth, or nose. Avoid using it on your face, underarms, or groin unless your doctor specifically tells you to. Do not use more than prescribed or for longer than your doctor recommends. Avoid using tight bandages or wraps over treated areas unless told to do so. Avoid using other steroid skin products on the same area at the same time without checking with your doctor first.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor if you notice any of the following: your skin condition is not improving after 2 weeks of treatment, your skin gets worse, you notice signs of skin infection such as increased redness, warmth, pus, or pain, you develop stretch marks, thinning skin, or easy bruising at the application site, you notice unusual weight gain, fatigue, or swelling in your face or ankles (which could be signs that the medicine is being absorbed into your body), or if a child using this medicine shows slow growth.
when_it_works: You may start to notice improvement in redness and itching within a few days of starting treatment. However, it may take 1 to 2 weeks to see the full benefit. Do not stop using it suddenly without talking to your doctor, even if you feel better.
special_populations: Children: Halobetasol should be used very carefully in children because their skin absorbs more of the medicine, which increases the risk of side effects. Use only under close medical supervision and for the shortest time possible. Pregnant or breastfeeding women: Talk to your doctor before using this medicine. It should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. If you are breastfeeding, avoid applying it to areas that may come in contact with your baby's skin or mouth. Elderly patients: Older adults may have thinner skin and may be more sensitive to the effects of this medicine. Use the smallest effective amount.
